abstract: Background Among fatalities due to parasitic diseases, deaths due to Leishmaniases rank second only to those caused by malaria. Endemic to 90 countries, more than a billion people are at risk of Leishmania infection. While there are no vaccines against Leishmaniases, treatments are available. However, the complexities of the treatment regimens, their high costs and toxic side effects, and most importantly the emerging problem of drug resistance, have continued to thrust forward research into this parasite’s cellular processes. The parasite is digenetic, reproducing by binary fission in both hosts, with DNA replication being central to the process. The absence of many conserved DNA replication proteins in Leishmania suggests the possibility of parasite-specific proteins being involved in the process. This investigation aimed to identify such proteins. Methods Using Leishmania donovani Cdc45, a component of the eukaryotic replicative helicase, as bait in immunoprecipitation reactions coupled to mass spectrometry, we looked for proteins that are a part of the Leishmania replisome. One of the promising candidates, annotated “hypothetical protein” in the Leishmania genome database, shared partial structural homology with Timeless of human, C. elegans and Drosophila , and hence we named it “LdTIM-like”. A second candidate, annotated “PIF1-like” in the genome database, was named “LdPIF6” based on sequence homology with T.brucei PIF6. Their possible involvement in DNA replication was examined by creating genomic knockouts and analyzing resultant phenotypes. Results LdTIM-like and LdPIF6 were constitutively nuclear, in keeping with a possible role in DNA replication. We found tim-like and pif6 were essential for parasite survival. Single allele knockouts lowered tim-like / pif6 expression significantly, and resulted in slower parasite growth. The mutant parasites took considerably longer to navigate S phase, and pulse-labelling with EdU revealed that the time taken by the mutant cell populations to complete DNA replication was significantly extended. The mutant parasites survived poorly in host macrophages as well. Conclusions Considering that these two proteins: LdTIM-like and LdPIF6, are essential to the parasite, coupled to their limited homology with human proteins, they could be investigated as potential sites for therapeutic intervention in future in-depth studies. Introduction
The diseases that are grouped as Leishmaniases are endemic to 90 countries, and are caused by ~ 20 species of the protozoan parasite
Leishmania.
Leishmaniases occur in three forms: cutaneous, mucocutaneous and visceral. While cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) is characterized by skin lesions, mucocutaneous leishmaniasis is typified by lesions in the skin and mucus membranes lining the throat, oral and nasal cavities. Visceral leishmaniasis (VL), on the other hand, is a systemic disease characterized by irregular bouts of fever, enlarged spleen and liver, and anaemia, and is fatal if not treated in a timely manner. Most CL cases are reported from the Mediterranean basin, Middle East and Central Asia while mucocutaneous leishmaniasis cases primarily occur in South America and East Africa. VL cases are usually found in Brazil, East Africa and the Indian subcontinent (
https://www.afro.who.int/health-topics/Leishmaniasis
). There are drugs to treat leishmaniasis, but due to emerging drug resistance as well as the toxicity of drugs that are presently in use, coupled to the absence of any vaccines against the disease, the search for new sites for therapeutic intervention continues.
Leishmania
parasites are digenetic, shuttling between the insect host where they exist extracellularly in the midgut and salivary glands as flagellate promastigotes (8–15 μm in length), and the mammalian host where they reside intracellularly in macrophages as aflagellate amastigotes (2–3 μm in length). Promastigotes and amastigotes reproduce asexually only, by binary fission, and DNA replication is central to this process.
DNA replication in eukaryotes is a highly conserved bipartite process, comprising of origin licensing occurring in G1 phase, and origin firing followed by continued DNA synthesis occurring in S phase [
1
]. Origin licensing is a complex multi-step process, beginning with the association of the Origin Recognition Complex (ORC, comprising Orc1-6) at or very near origin DNA in late mitosis/early G1, followed by the landing of Cdc6 and Cdt1 proteins on this origin-bound ORC in G1 phase, and culminating with the association of the MCM double hexamer (each MCM hexamer is an annular complex of six MCM subunits: Mcm2-7). The licensed origins are empowered to fire as the cells enter S phase when Cdc45 and GINS associate with the MCM double hexamer, an interaction which ultimately ends with the split of the double hexamer into two MCM hexamers each associated with Cdc45 and GINS. This is followed by each Cdc45-MCM-GINS (CMG) complex ejecting one strand of the duplex, such that the two opposing CMGs now each encircle only the leading strand template [
2
,
3
]. The CMG complex is the replicative helicase, and as origins fire the two complexes move in opposite directions along the leading strand templates, unwinding DNA with the advancing of the replication forks.
The loading of Cdc45 and GINS onto the MCM double hexamer has long been known to require Cdc6 and Cdt1. More recently, another protein named DONSON has been identified to play a role in CMG formation and stabilization in vertebrates, and is believed to deliver and dock GINS (but not Cdc45) on the MCM double hexamer assembled at the origin [
4
–
6
]. DONSON is essential for replication initiation but not fork elongation. The essential replicative DNA polymerases (DNA pol ε, DNA pol δ and DNA pol α) as well as other protein factors such as yeast Ctf4/human AND-1 (the homotrimer which associates with Cdc45 and GINS and serves as a recruitment platform for other replication proteins), Timeless-Tipin (the metazoan orthologs of the yeast Tof1 and Csm3 proteins; Timeless-Tipin heterodimer strengthens the interaction of the MCM core helicase with its DNA substrate by acting as an extension bridge between the two), and Claspin (the metazoan ortholog of yeast Mrc1; Claspin plays a role in mediating the replication stress response), that are a part of the advancing eukaryotic replisome, act concertedly to ensure the efficient synthesis of DNA [
7
,
8
].
While the process of DNA replication is broadly conserved in
Leishmania
species as well as other trypanosomatids (whose family
Leishmania
belongs to), several players are absent or remain unidentified in these organisms. The ORC in
Trypanosoma brucei
has been characterized, and is somewhat divergent, carrying ORC1 and ORC4 along with two parasite proteins Tb3120 and Tb7980 which share weak homology with Orc2 and Orc5 respectively [
9
]. ORC1, as well as the orthologs of TbORC4, Tb3120 and Tb7980 are present in
Leishmania
species as well. Orc3 and Orc6 are absent in trypanosomatids, and no distinct Cdc6 is present, with ORC1 being partly conserved with the yeast Cdc6 and therefore being annotated as ORC1/CDC6. While we have been able to identify a putative AND-1 in these organisms using sequence homology searches, Cdt1, DONSON, Timeless-Tipin and Claspin have been unidentifiable. The absence of many of the orthologs of conserved eukaryotic replication proteins suggests that the replication machinery in trypanosomatids may be simpler than in other eukaryotes, while also suggesting that parasite-specific proteins may be involved in the process.
The present study was undertaken with the aim of identifying trypanosomatid-specific/
Leishmania
-specific proteins that might be involved in DNA replication. Using the
Leishmania donovani
Cdc45 protein as bait in immunoprecipitation reactions followed by mass spectrometry analysis of the immunoprecipitates, we identified two candidate proteins which are the
Leishmania donovani
1 S orthologs of LdBPK_161620 and LdBPK_211430, that consistently co-immunoprecipitated with Cdc45. Using the approach of creating genomic knockouts of the genes encoding these two candidates and characterizing the phenotypes obtained, we found that both genes are essential for cell survival. Decrease in gene dosage leads to significantly lower levels of transcripts of the respective genes, slower parasite growth, slower navigation of cells across S phase, and extended span period of DNA replication of the population. Taken together, the results of this study suggest that the Ld1S orthologs of LdBPK_161620 and LdBPK_211430 are involved in the replication of
Leishmania donovani
DNA.

Identification of Cdc45-interacting proteins
As an integral component of the replicative helicase, Cdc45 is involved in both, replication initiation as well as elongation of the new DNA chains being synthesized. Previous work from our laboratory has demonstrated
L. donovani cdc45
to be essential for cell survival [
19
]. In our search for possible
Leishmania
-specific proteins involved in DNA replication we started with using Cdc45 as the bait, looking for proteins that interact with it. Thus, whole cell lysates were isolated from
Leishmania
promastigotes expressing Cdc45-FLAG [
19
], and the FLAG-tagged protein immunoprecipitated from these lysates using anti-FLAG M2 agarose beads (Methods, Fig.
1
A). The immunoprecipitated fraction was analyzed by LC-MS as outlined (Methods, Fig.
1
B). The experiment was performed five times: four experiments were performed using logarithmically growing promastigotes, and the fifth experiment was performed with hydroxyurea (HU)-synchronized promastigotes, three hours after release from HU-induced G1/S arrest. These synchronized cells would almost all be at a stage of active DNA replication. In every experiment, simultaneous immunoprecipitations carried out with lysates isolated from similarly treated
Leishmania
promastigotes harboring empty vector, served as control. The data were analyzed against the proteome data of the
Leishmania donovani
reference strain LdBPK282A1 (available in
www.tritrypdb.org
) as data for
Leishmania donovani
1 S is not available. Known eukaryotic replication proteins that co-immunoprecipitated with Cdc45 included MCM components and DNA pol ε (Additional file 1: Table
S1
). As Cdc45 does not directly interact with ORC at the origin at any stage, it was not surprising that none of the ORC components co-immunoprecipitated with Cdc45. Surprisingly, proteins annotated as GINS components in trypanosomatids did not co-immunoprecipitate with Cdc45 in any of the experiments. While the reason for this remains unknown, it is possible that GINS interacts stably with Cdc45 only on DNA template, and the treatment of the lysates with DNase I prior to immunoprecipitation may destabilize the interaction. The pre-treatment of lysates with DNase I may be the reason for our failure to detect other proteins known to be a part of the advancing replisome.

Partial depletion of LdTIM-like and LdPIF6 negatively impacts parasite survival in host macrophages
Leishmania
parasites cycle between the insect host and mammalian host. In the insect host the parasites exist extracellularly as motile promastigotes. Early-stage promastigotes, called procyclics, reside in the insect midgut. Procyclics eventually differentiate into metacyclic promastigotes which migrate to the salivary glands. These metacyclics have the capability of infecting the human host cell. Once released into the mammalian host bloodstream through the insect bite these metacyclics are taken up by macrophages, within which they differentiate into non-motile amastigotes. The intracellular environment of macrophages is hostile to parasite survival, and the oxidative burst the parasite faces within the macrophage is designed to eliminate the parasite. The parasite, however, has devised multiple ways to survive the onslaught, and if successful, is able to establish infection. Within the macrophage the parasite reproduces asexually by binary fission. To examine the impact of partial depletion of LdTIM-like and LdPIF6 on parasite survival and propagation within host macrophages, J774A.1 murine macrophages were infected with
Leishmania
metacyclics (wild type,
tim-like
−/+
and
pif6
−/+

8
, 5 h time-point), thus confirming that partial depletion of either protein was not affecting the ability of either mutant parasite to infect the host cell. However, the intracellular mutant parasite loads dropped subsequently and were sizably lower than wild type parasite load by 48 h after infection in both cases, implying that LdTIM-like and LdPIF6 may modulate DNA replication events in the amastigote form as well (Fig.
8
, 48 h time-point).

Discussion
While eukaryotic DNA replication is largely conserved, with multiple origins of replication on each chromosome and the main protein players found across all eukaryotes, trypanosomatids are early diverging eukaryotes and several of the conserved proteins are absent in these organisms. Furthermore, while
Trypanosoma
species carry multiple origins on each chromosome, they carry relatively fewer origins than other eukaryotes [
31
,
32
].
Trypanosoma
and
Leishmania
species are also distinct, in that
Trypanosoma
chromosomes have multiple active origins and several dormant (licensed to fire) origins, while
Leishmania
chromosomes exhibit the unusual feature of having one primary active origin per chromosome, with several additional initiation sites as well [
33
,
34
]. The
Leishmania
genome exhibits one more unusual feature: the replication of parts of its genome (subtelomeric regions of chromosomes) extends into G2/M phase [
35
].
In the absence of many of the conserved eukaryotic replication proteins in
Leishmania
species, such as Orc3, Orc6, Cdt1, geminin, Timeless (which was not identifiable by sequence homology and thus believed to be absent at the time of initiation of this study) and Tipin, we initiated this study with the aim of exploring the possibility of parasite-specific proteins being involved in
Leishmania
DNA replication. Cdc45 is an integral component of the eukaryotic DNA replication machinery, and cryo-EM studies analyzing yeast replisome architecture and dynamics at origin DNA find that formation of CMG splits the MCM double hexamer at the licensed origin into individual partially separated hexamers, each associated with Cdc45 and GINS to which DNA pol ε is recruited. The double CMGE which are partially separated nucleate DNA melting at the origin. This is followed by the association of Mcm10 which culminates in the complete separation of the two CMGE complexes and ejection of the lagging strand template DNAs. Thus, the replisomes advance along the leading strand template on either side of the bidirectional origin [
36
,
37
].
Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Cdc45
ts
mutants harboring mutations in the domains that mediate interactions with MCM and GINS subunits display impaired S phase progression and poor fidelity of DNA replication at the non-permissive temperature [
38
]. Overexpression of Cdc45 in colorectal cancer cell lines triggers activation of additional origins and this is coupled to whole chromosomal instability [
39
]. Genome instability is one of the characteristic features of cancer progression. Many cancers displaying chromosomal instability show elevated expression of Cdc45, suggesting that chromosomal instability may be at least in part a consequence of perturbation of Cdc45 levels. Work from our laboratory has demonstrated that depletion of
Leishmania
Cdc45 leads to defects in DNA replication. Furthermore, our work demonstrated that Cdc45 interacted with the polymerase clamp protein PCNA through its PIP box, an interaction that is essential for cell survival, implicating a role for Cdc45 in stabilizing the replicative polymerase at the replication fork via PCNA interactions [
19
]. Considering the central role of Cdc45 in replication initiation as well as elongation we used Cdc45 to fish out other proteins that may be involved in
Leishmania
DNA replication. The two most promising candidates that were selected based on their reproducible enrichment in multiple experiments (Fig.
1
C) were the Ld1S orthologs of LdBPK_161620 and LdBPK_211430, and although we were unable to validate the interaction of Cdc45 with each of these two proteins using immunoprecipitation experiments due to the non-availability of antibodies, we proceeded with evaluating their possible involvement in DNA replication.
The protein encoded by the Ld1S ortholog of LdBPK_161620 did not share significant amino acid sequence homology with any other protein across eukaryotes. This candidate was, however, found to be in part structurally homologous to the eukaryotic Timeless protein (Fig.
2
B), with almost 50% of the protein sharing homology with Timeless of multiple eukaryotes (Fig.
2
A), and hence we named it LdTIM-like. LdTIM-like was found to be constitutively nuclear (Fig.
3
C), though not expressed to the same extent at all stages of cell cycle: it was strongly expressed in G1 and S, less so in early G2, and only weakly expressed in late G2/M and post-mitotic cells (Fig.
3
C). This pattern of expression somewhat resembled that of the human Timeless protein that has been found to be highly enriched in S and G2 phases [
29
]. Our inability to create genomic nulls of
tim-like
suggested that it is essential for cell survival (Figure S
4
), although this needs to be corroborated by carrying out plasmid loss experiments with the
tim-like
−/+
::TIM-like
+
cells in absence of drug selection pressure, to determine if the surviving population maintains the plasmid or not. These experiments are currently underway. Knockout of one allele was accompanied by a significant drop in transcript levels (Fig.
4
A). These levels, while sufficient to support cell survival, were insufficient to maintain the same rates of growth (Fig.
4
C).
tim-like
−/+
parasites navigated S phase slower than usual (Fig.
5
B), and the
tim-like
−/+
population had an extended period of DNA replication (Fig.
6
B and C). Although the structural homology of LdTIM-like with Timeless suggests it might be the
Leishmania
ortholog of Timeless, given that only about 50% of the
Leishmania
protein shares homology with Timeless it is difficult to gauge how conserved with Timeless it may be in function. While the CMG complex is the primary replicative helicase responsible for unwinding DNA as the fork progresses, the replisome oftentimes faces barriers such as unusual secondary structures/DNA lesions due to damage/protein-DNA complexes, and these challenges can lead to fork stalling and eventual fork collapse. To ensure genomic stability these obstacles are combated by Timeless-Tipin (the metazoan orthologs of the yeast proteins Tof1 and Csm3) which lie ahead of the MCM complex at the leading edge of the advancing replisome [
7
]. Timeless-Tipin has been proposed to act as a “molecular brake”, slowing down the replication fork at fork barriers and either allowing a safe restart of the paused fork or promoting recombination at the fork barrier, based on the type of barrier it is facing [
40
]. Further detailed investigations are necessary to ascertain if LdTIM-like plays a similar role.
LdBPK_211430 was found to be annotated as PIF1-like in the
Leishmania donovani
reference strain genome sequence (Tritryp database). While PIF helicases are conserved across eukaryotes, the number of PIF helicases varies across organisms.
S. cerevisiae
has two PIF helicases: ScPif1p and ScRrm3p, both of which are mitochondrial as well as nuclear.
S. pombe
and humans have only one PIF helicase.
T. brucei
has eight PIF proteins that share homology with the ScPIF1. Sequence analysis revealed that LdBPK_211430 is the ortholog of TbPIF6 (Figure S
2
), and thus we considered its Ld1S ortholog to be LdPIF6. Seven of the eight
T. brucei
PIFs were found to be conserved in
Leishmania
species: the ortholog of TbPIF5 is absent. Analysis of the subcellular localization of LdPIF6 revealed it to be constitutively nuclear, being more or less equivalently expressed at all cell cycle stages (Fig.
3
D). While six of the
T. brucei
PIFs: TbPIF1, TbPIF2, TbPIF4, TbPIF5, TbPIF7 and TbPIF8, are mitochondrial, TbPIF6 is the only nuclear TbPIF [
21
]. The nuclear localization of LdPIF6 is in keeping with a role in DNA replication or/and repair. Although our results with LdPIF6 also suggest that the gene is essential (Figure S
5
), efforts are ongoing to confirm this using plasmid loss assays. No genomic null of TbPIF6 has been reported, and single allele knockout of TbPIF6 as well as RNAi knockdown of TbPIF6 survived with no apparent growth defects, however, the extent of downregulation of TbPIF6 expression in these experiments has not been reported [
21
]. RNAi studies revealed TbPIF1, TbPIF2 and TbPIF8 to be essential for cell survival, while the survival of TbPIF3 and TbPIF7 genomic nulls signified their non-essential nature. We found
Ldpif6
−/+
cells to grow slower than wild type cells, and these cells took longer than usual to progress across S phase (Figs.
4
D and
5
C). Furthermore, DNA replication in this population of cells too was more protracted (Fig.
7
A and B), suggesting a role for LdPIF6 in DNA replication in these parasites. While the nuclear ScPif1 has been proposed to play a role in the maturation of Okazaki fragments [
41
], ScRrm3 moves with the elongating replication fork, and is proposed to remove barriers to fork advance such as DNA quadriplex structures, thus promoting genomic stability [
42
]. A more in-depth analysis will have to be carried out to investigate the nature of LdPIF6’s role in modulating DNA replication.
In treating cancers, several chemotherapeutic agents target DNA replication machinery, on the basis of the premise that inhibitors of DNA replication will slow down/hamper cell proliferation. Extending the same premise to
Leishmania
parasites, targeting parasite-specific components of the DNA replication machinery may serve to subjugate the parasite population. This study was undertaken with the long-term aim of determining if any
Leishmania
-specific proteins involved in DNA replication can serve as sites for therapeutic intervention. LdTIM-like shares very limited sequence identity (17% identity over 47% coverage) with human Timeless, and only ~ 50% of the
Leishmania
protein shares structural homology with human Timeless. This suggests that the structurally non-conserved C-terminal part of LdTIM-like may be a potential region that could be tested. LdPIF6 shares almost 40% identity with human PIF1, but over 58% coverage only. However, further in-depth investigations including high throughput small molecule drug screens need to be carried out to examine the potential of these two proteins (or parts thereof) as targets for clinical intervention. Furthermore, while this study indicates the involvement of LdTIM-like and LdPIF6 in
Leishmania
DNA replication, it has not unravelled the mechanisms by which they both may act. As part of the CMG complex Cdc45 is essential for the initiation of DNA replication as well as the elongation of DNA chains being synthesized. Whether LdTIM-like and LdPIF6 are part of the replication initiation process, chain elongation process, or both, remains to be worked out.
